long-haul = travelling a very long distance by air, often between continents
layover = a wait at an airport between two parts of a journey
turbulence = sudden rough movement of a plane caused by air currents
rush hour = the busy time of day when many people travel to or from work
connecting flight = a second flight that you take after changing planes
charter flight = a flight hired for a tour group, not a regular scheduled service
low-cost airline = an airline that sells cheap tickets and charges extra for many services
boarding gate = the door and waiting area where you enter the plane
cabin baggage = bags you take into the cabin rather than putting in the hold
excess baggage = luggage heavier or larger than the airline's free limit, charged extra
baggage allowance = the weight or number of bags you may take without extra fees
overhead locker = the compartment above the seats for cabin bags
frequent-flyer programme = a scheme that gives points or upgrades to regular passengers
upgrade = a move to a more comfortable class of seat, sometimes free
economy class = the cheapest, most basic seats on a plane
business class = a more expensive cabin with extra space and service
red-eye flight = an overnight flight that arrives early in the morning
missed connection = failing to catch the next plane, train or bus in time
airbridge = a movable corridor that connects the terminal to the aircraft door
in-flight service = food, drink and help offered by cabin crew during a flight
duty-free = goods sold without tax at airports or on planes and ships
departure board = the screen listing times and gates for leaving flights or trains
check-in desk = the counter where you show your ticket and leave hold luggage
e-ticket = a ticket stored on a phone or in an email, not printed on thick card
off-peak = at a less busy and often cheaper time to travel
congestion charge = a fee for driving into a crowded city centre at busy times
tailback = a long line of slow or stopped traffic
roadworks = repairs or building work on a road that slow traffic
diversion = a different route you must take because a road is closed
toll road = a road you pay to drive on
dual carriageway = a fast road with a strip of land between the two directions
hard shoulder = the strip at the edge of a motorway for stopping in an emergency
bypass = a road that takes traffic around a town instead of through the centre
slip road = a short road that joins or leaves a motorway
satnav = a device or app that gives driving directions using satellites
breakdown cover = insurance that sends help if your car stops working
puncture = a hole in a tyre that lets the air out
spare tyre = an extra tyre carried in a vehicle in case one fails
car hire = paying to use a car for a short period
international driving permit = an extra document that translates your licence for use abroad
ferry crossing = a journey by boat that carries people and often cars across water
shuttle bus = a bus that runs back and forth between two points, such as a hotel and an airport
park and ride = a car park outside a city with a bus into the centre
high-speed rail = trains that travel much faster than ordinary services
sleeper train = a night train with beds so you travel while you sleep
buffet car = the carriage on a train where you can buy drinks and snacks
hitchhiking = travelling by asking drivers to take you for free
car sharing = several people travelling in one car to cut cost and traffic
express coach = a long-distance bus that makes few stops
cycle path = a route for bicycles, often separated from cars
B&B = a small guesthouse that includes breakfast in the price
self-catering = accommodation with a kitchen so you cook your own meals
overbooking = accepting more reservations than there are rooms or seats
half board = a hotel deal that includes breakfast and one other meal
full board = a hotel deal that includes breakfast, lunch and dinner
en suite = a bedroom with its own private bathroom attached
boutique hotel = a small, stylish hotel, often with an individual design
holiday let = a flat or house rented to tourists for a short stay
timeshare = a scheme where you buy the right to use a holiday property for a set week each year
glamping = camping with extra comfort, such as a proper bed or a cabin
chalet = a wooden house, often in the mountains, used as holiday accommodation
villa = a large, often detached holiday house, typically in a warm country
cottage = a small house in the countryside, often rented to visitors
caravan = a home on wheels that a car can pull, used for holidays
camper van = a van fitted with beds and a small kitchen for travelling
concierge = a hotel employee who helps guests with bookings, tickets and local advice
housekeeping = the staff or service that cleans hotel rooms
minibar = a small fridge in a hotel room with drinks and snacks for sale
late checkout = permission to leave a hotel room later than the usual time
early check-in = being allowed to take a room before the usual arrival time
no-show = a person who has a booking but does not arrive
non-refundable = a booking you cannot cancel in order to get your money back
cancellation policy = the rules about whether you get money back if you cancel
booking confirmation = a message or document that proves your reservation is accepted
room rate = the price charged for a hotel room for a night
tourist tax = a small local charge added to a hotel bill per person or night
key card = a plastic card that opens a hotel room instead of a metal key
wake-up call = a phone call from the hotel to wake you at a chosen time
hotel chain = a group of hotels with the same brand in many places
occupancy = how full a hotel is; the number of rooms in use
itinerary = a detailed list of places, times and transport for a trip
sightseeing = visiting famous buildings and places as a tourist
package holiday = a holiday in which flights and accommodation are booked together
all-inclusive = a holiday price that covers meals, drinks and many activities
backpacking = travelling cheaply with a rucksack, often for a long period
off the beaten track = in places that few tourists visit
eco-tourism = tourism designed to protect nature and support local people
carbon offset = a payment meant to balance the emissions from a journey, for example by planting trees
sustainable tourism = travel that tries not to harm the environment or local communities
overtourism = when too many visitors damage a place or make life hard for residents
mass tourism = large numbers of people visiting the same popular places
cultural tourism = travel focused on history, art, festivals and local traditions
adventure tourism = holidays based on physical challenge, such as trekking or rafting
agritourism = holidays on working farms, often with local food and rural tasks
city break = a short holiday in a city, often a weekend
guided tour = a visit around a place with someone who explains what you see
excursion = a short trip, often from a hotel or cruise, to see a nearby place
cruise = a holiday on a large ship that visits several ports
tour operator = a company that designs and sells complete holidays
travel agent's = a shop that advises on and books holidays and tickets
holiday rep = a person employed by a tour company to look after guests at a resort
single supplement = extra money charged when one person occupies a room meant for two
peak season = the most popular, usually most expensive, time to visit a place
out of season = at the time of year when a destination is quiet and often cheaper
high season = the busiest holiday period, when prices and crowds are at their height
low season = the least busy period, when prices tend to fall
last-minute deal = a cheap holiday sold shortly before departure
tourist trap = a place that charges too much because visitors do not know better
tourist attraction = a place that visitors come to see
heritage site = a place protected because of its historical or cultural importance
hidden gem = an excellent place that few tourists have discovered
unspoilt = not damaged or made ugly by development or crowds
picturesque = attractive in a way that looks like a painting
hop-on hop-off = a tourist bus you can leave and rejoin at many stops with one ticket
audio guide = a recorded commentary you listen to while visiting a museum or site
admission fee = the money you pay to enter a museum, park or attraction
skip-the-line = a ticket that lets you enter without waiting in the ordinary queue
backpacker = a person who travels cheaply with a rucksack, often staying in hostels
working holiday = a trip abroad in which you work for part of the time, often on a special visa
travel brochure = a colourful booklet advertising holidays and destinations
tourist information centre = an office that gives maps, advice and tickets to visitors
optional extra = an activity or service not included in the basic holiday price
shoulder season = the weeks just before or after high season, often quieter and cheaper
touristy = full of visitors and souvenir shops; not very local or authentic
overcrowded = with far too many people in a place
breathtaking = extremely impressive or beautiful
old town = the historic central district of a city, often with old streets
viewpoint = a place from which you can see a wide or famous view
waymarked = a path marked with signs or coloured flashes so walkers do not get lost
authentic = real and typical of a place, not invented only for tourists
jet lag = tiredness and confusion after a long flight across time zones
lost luggage = bags that the airline cannot find after a flight
travel insurance = a policy that pays if you fall ill, cancel, or lose bags abroad
delay = a situation in which a plane, train or bus leaves or arrives later than planned
cancelled flight = a flight that will not operate as planned
transport strike = when transport workers stop work, so trains, buses or planes do not run normally
lost passport = a passport that you cannot find while you are travelling
pickpocket = a thief who steals from bags or pockets in crowds
embassy = the office of one country in another that helps its citizens and represents its government
consulate = a smaller official office abroad that helps travellers with documents and emergencies
visa = an official permission, often a stamp or document, to enter a country
transit visa = permission to pass through a country on the way to another destination
e-visa = a visa you apply for and receive online rather than in a passport sticker
biometric passport = a passport with a chip storing a photograph and other identity data
customs declaration = a form stating what goods you are bringing into a country
confiscate = to officially take something away, for example at security or customs
insurance claim = a formal request for an insurer to pay for a loss
excess = the first amount of a loss that you pay yourself under an insurance policy
flight compensation = money an airline may owe you after a long delay or cancellation
diverted = sent to a different airport than the one on the ticket
stranded = unable to continue a journey, often because of cancelled transport
tourist scam = a trick designed to take money from visitors who do not know local prices or rules
unlicensed taxi = a private car that offers rides without official permission
seasickness = feeling ill because of the movement of a boat
airsickness = feeling ill because of the movement of a plane
foreign currency = the money used in another country
bureau de change = an office that exchanges one currency for another
traveller's cheques = paper cheques bought in advance that can be cashed abroad
prepaid card = a card you load with money before you travel, then spend abroad
travel adapter = a plug that lets you use electrical devices in another country's sockets
luggage tag = a label on a suitcase with your name and contact details
money belt = a hidden pouch worn under clothes to keep cash and documents safe
boarding pass = the document you show to get on a plane
passport = an official document that identifies you and lets you travel abroad
visa application = the form and process of asking a country for permission to enter
border requirements = the documents and rules you must meet to cross into a country
travel documents = the papers you need for a trip, such as a passport, visa and tickets
travel advisory = official government advice about safety in a country
weather disruption = delays or cancellations caused by storms, snow, fog or heat
delayed baggage = suitcases that arrive later than the passenger
damaged suitcase = a bag that has been broken or torn during a journey
rerouted = sent on a different path or via different cities than planned
Schengen visa = a visa that allows short stays in the group of European countries that share open borders
emergency passport = a temporary travel document issued when your passport is lost or stolen
time zone = a region of the world that uses the same clock time
passport validity = how much time is left before a passport expires
hold luggage = suitcases put in the aircraft hold, not carried into the cabin
liquid restrictions = airport security rules that limit how much liquid you may take into the cabin
priority boarding = the right to get on the plane before other passengers
denied boarding = not being allowed on a plane, often because it is overbooked
